sections.report:
**Walk (working notes)**

First read: the eye lands on the bold "Notes for ferry passengers" at the top left, then moves down a single narrow column of plain text broken up by three bold subheads. It reads as a help or info page for passengers of a local river ferry. It feels calm, plain and functional. The right half of the frame is empty. The page runs past the bottom edge at "Winter service", so this is one screen of a longer page.

Job (assumed): a web page where passengers find out how the ferry runs, how to board, how to buy tickets, and what changes in winter.

- Can a first-time viewer say in one sentence what it's for? **yes**
- Do the main image and headline make one idea? **yes** (there is no image, so the line does not apply)
- Does every element do a job? **yes** (there are no boxes, rules or ornaments; the bullets carry a real list)
- Do type, colour and shape share one mood? **yes**
- Is the copy finished, with no placeholders or typos? **yes**
- Does each kind of element look the same everywhere? **yes** (the three subheads match, and so do the body paragraphs)
- Do colour, shape and direction carry the right mood? **yes** (sober black on white suits a practical notice)
- Does each heading name what its section holds? **yes**

Every line is yes, so step 5 had no entries to open. Copy read as a stranger would: the timing and ticket lines leave out the facts a passenger acts on. No checklist line covers that, so I report it as an extra finding.

---

**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
None. Every line is yes.

One extra copy finding that no checklist line covers. It is about details a viewer acts on, so I pass it on:

1. **Timings and the pass term are vague where the passenger needs exact facts** (copy, not a checklist line). Where: the opening paragraph at about y 125–170 ("every forty minutes between early morning and late evening"), the Winter service paragraph at about y 785+ ("thins to one boat each hour, and the last…"), and the season pass line at about y 670–715 ("for a month").
   - What the viewer meets: they can't plan a crossing. They don't know when the first and last boats leave, or which minutes past the hour the 40-minute cycle runs from. "For a month" can mean a calendar month or 30 days from purchase, and the passenger will hold the operator to whichever reading they took.
   - Why: under the critic's guidance, a time or term that can be read two ways is a defect.
   - Fix: give the first and last departure times from each landing, or link to the timetable from the opening paragraph. Say when winter starts and ends. Say exactly what period the pass covers.
   - Type and weight: defect, major. On a passenger notes page, planning a trip is the main job.

**What's working.**
- The page holds together as one sober notice. It uses one typeface, black on white, and nothing decorative. That suits a practical page about a public service, and nothing pulls the eye away from the content.
- The three subheads ("Boarding", "Tickets", "Winter service") say exactly what their sections hold, so a passenger can scan to the one they need.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- The page continues below the frame (cut off mid-sentence at "Winter service"). Whether the rest has a timetable, prices or contact details changes how serious the vagueness finding is. Check the full page.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Walk (working notes)**
First read: the eye lands on "Notes for ferry passengers" at top left. It then moves down through the bold headings "Boarding", "Tickets" and "Winter service". This is a plain info page for ferry riders, and it feels calm and tidy.
Job (assumed): a reference page that lets passengers scan for the topic they need.
- One element dominates? **yes**. The title is about 38 px and bold, roughly twice the body size, and it's the only element at that size.
- Each text level distinct, no near-identical sizes? **yes**. I see three sizes: title about 38 px, headings about 22 px bold, body about 18 px, plus bullets at body size. The heading-to-body step is fairly small, but the bold weight separates the levels at a glance.
- Headings differ in more than size? **yes**. They're bold, and the body is regular.

No line came out `no` or `unsure`, so I didn't need to open any entries.

---

**Section.** What matters first (hierarchy): applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The title clearly leads.** "Notes for ferry passengers" (about x 120–593, y 60–98) is about twice the body size and heavy. It's the only thing at that level, so the eye knows where to start and what the page is right away.
- **Headings use size and weight together.** "Boarding" (y≈293), "Tickets" (y≈564) and "Winter service" (y≈759) are only a little larger than the body text, but they're bold. That keeps the scale down to three sizes and still makes the topics easy to scan. Each heading also sits closer to its own text than to the block above, so it reads as the label for what follows.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure.

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is the space inside each group clearly smaller than the space between groups, so each heading sits nearer the text it introduces?**
   - **Where:** Each heading sits about 10 px above its own text, so it attaches downward correctly. But the gap above a heading is no bigger than the gap between two paragraphs inside a section:
     - About 34 px above "Boarding" (y≈250→284).
     - About 32 px above "Tickets" (y≈522→554).
     - About 36 px between "…upstream side." and "Riders with bicycles…" (y≈337→373).
   - **What the viewer gets:** The page reads as one even run of paragraphs. When a passenger scans for "Tickets" or "Winter service", the sections don't separate, and the end of the bullet list runs straight into "Tickets".
   - **Why:** Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. II, on grouping by proximity (Wertheimer). Bringhurst, *Elements of Typographic Style* §2.2.2, on more space above a subhead than below.
   - **Fix:** Either open the space above each H2 to clearly more than the paragraph gap (roughly 1.5–2×), or tighten the paragraph gap, so each section reads as one block.
   - Defect. Major, because this is a page people scan by section.
2. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side that makes the page look about to tip?** / **Is the empty space gathered into a few deliberate areas?** / **Do the main divisions of the frame follow one proportion?**
   - **Where:** The text column covers about x 120–675 of a 1280 px frame. Everything from x≈680 to the right edge is empty.
   - **What the viewer gets:** The empty space is all in one place, but nothing gives it a job. The page looks lopsided, as if a sidebar or picture failed to load or the layout was never set for a wide screen. The 120 px left margin against a roughly 600 px right void doesn't follow any proportion.
   - **Why:** Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance". Tschichold, *The New Typography*, and Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems*, on negative space being shaped on purpose and not left over.
   - **Fix:** Keep the line length, which is good. Either centre the column in the frame, or give the right side something to do: a timetable or a "quick facts" panel would suit this page. Or set the left margin as a clear share of the frame so the asymmetry looks chosen.
   - **What would make it fine:** If the right side is a slot that didn't load in the capture, this isn't a finding.
   - Taste/convention. Minor: the text still reads, but the page looks unfinished.

**What's working.**
- Strict single left edge: the title, paragraphs and headings all hang on x≈120, and the bullets indent cleanly to x≈144. Nothing nearly lines up and misses, so the column feels orderly and the eye path is plain top to bottom.
- Each heading sits tight to its own text (about 10 px), so no heading floats between sections. Only the space above them needs to grow.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 9 yes, 4 no (space inside group smaller than between groups; empty space gathered and deliberate; visual weight balances; main divisions follow one proportion)

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do paragraphs and columns break cleanly, with no lone short word on a last line?** The first paragraph under "Tickets" ends with "kiosk." alone on its last line (x≈120, y≈627). A one-word last line makes a short two-line paragraph look broken and adds a nearly empty line of white between "Tickets" and the season-pass paragraph. That makes the Tickets section look looser than Boarding above it. Source: Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*, section 2.4.2. Fix: bring a second word down to the last line, for example with a non-breaking space between "landing" and "kiosk" or `text-wrap: pretty` on paragraphs. Rewording the sentence slightly also works. Convention. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- The body text is set well for reading. It uses one plain sans in near-black on white at what looks like about 17 px with generous leading (about 1.6). The measure is held to roughly 60–65 characters (for example, "The river ferry runs from the north landing to the market quay"), right in Bringhurst's 45–75 range. Keep the narrow column even if the empty right half of the canvas gets used for something else.
- The text is broken into clear sections. Bold subheads (Boarding, Tickets, Winter service) come from the same family, and the three boarding rules are pulled out into a short bulleted list. A passenger can scan for the one thing they need without reading every paragraph.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The "Winter service" paragraph is cut off at the bottom edge (y≈795). This is almost certainly where the screenshot's viewport ends, not clipping in the design. Scroll the live page to confirm the text shows in full.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (paragraphs break cleanly with no lone last word).

Walk (working notes): the image is one screen (1280×800), so I worked from the whole image. Bash was refused, so I couldn't run the crop script.
First read: the eye lands on the bold black title, then moves down the left column of text. It reads as a plain, calm information page for ferry passengers.
Color lines:
- Small palette: yes. Near-black text on white, no hue.
- Saturated color kept small: yes. There is none.
- Value range and grayscale structure: yes. The structure is black on white, carried by weight and size.
- Warm/cool: yes. No temperature is used.
- Matching colors look the same: yes. All text is one near-black.
- No vibrating edges: yes.
- Status colors: yes. None.
- Color alone carrying meaning: yes. None.
- Dark theme: yes. It isn't one.

No line is no or unsure, so there are no entries to open.

**Section.** Color: applies. The page is fully neutral (near-black text on a white background, no hue), so most lines pass because nothing in them is present.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.** The page uses only near-black on white, so value carries all the structure. The title, section heads ("Boarding", "Tickets", "Winter service") and body text stay distinct in grayscale through size and weight alone. Nothing competes with the text, which suits a page people read to learn how to board and pay. The text looks like a softened near-black rather than pure #000, which keeps the contrast high without being harsh.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes.
